passages.t: ‘Contend with my opponents, O LORD’, and those who hate without cause
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). He asks God to fight for him. “Contend with my opponents, O LORD; fight against those who fight against me” (verse 1). “Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid” (verse 2). Above all he wants to hear God say to him, “I am your salvation” (verse 3).

He asks that his enemies fall into their own traps: “For without cause they laid their net for me” (verse 7).

The middle of the psalm is the saddest part. These were people he had cared for. “Yet when they were ill, I put on sackcloth; I humbled myself with fasting” (verse 13). He grieved for them “like one mourning for his mother” (verse 14). But when he stumbled, “they assembled in glee” (verse 15).

He cries, “How long, O Lord, will You look on?” (verse 17). And he asks God, “do not let them gloat over me” (verse 24). It ends in praise: “Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Two pictures run through the psalm: a battle and a court. ‘Contend’ in verse 1 is a word for bringing a legal case. ‘Hostile witnesses’ come forward with charges he knows nothing about (verse 11). He wants God to be both his warrior and his lawyer.

Israel's law punished a false witness with the harm he had tried to bring on the accused: “you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother” (Deuteronomy 19:19). When the psalmist prays that his enemies fall into their own net, he is asking for exactly that justice.

Sackcloth and fasting (verse 13) were signs of grief and prayer. He had mourned for these people when they were sick. The betrayal is worse because the love was real.
passages.later:
Jesus said of those who rejected him, “this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’” (John 15:25). The words come from verse 19 of this psalm or from Psalm 69:4, which say the same.

Jesus also faced false witnesses at his trial (Matthew 26:59-60). And he taught the opposite of gloating: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).
passages.hard: Verses 4 to 8 ask God to bring ruin on enemies. This is one of the prayers the book page discusses in ‘The cursing psalms’, with the ways Christians read them. No reading of this psalm makes it right to harm anyone.
passages.asks:
Has someone you cared for turned against you? The psalm gives you words for that particular pain, and lets you hand the case to God instead of fighting it yourself.

Notice also verse 13. Before he prayed against them, he had prayed for them. The psalm asks whether you have done the same.
